Baby & Child

Helping a child after a baby brother or sister dies

Updated: November 11, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

When a baby dies during pregnancy or after birth, another child in the family may also need help understanding what has happened. They may be grieving a sibling they knew or the future they imagined together. While coping with your own loss, you do not have to find perfect words. A familiar adult, truthful explanations and repeated opportunities to talk can help your child feel included and cared for.

Tell them gently, without waiting for perfect words

Choose a quiet moment with someone the child trusts and explain what has happened as soon as reasonably possible. A short conversation is enough to begin. If you cannot manage it alone, ask a familiar adult to sit with you or help tell them. Arrange to return to the conversation rather than leaving the child to piece together overheard fragments.

Start with what the child already knows about the baby. Use the baby’s name if that feels right for your family. Give a little information, pause and let their questions guide the next part. A child who never met the baby can still feel a loss; their place in the family does not depend on having shared photographs or memories.

Use clear words for death

Words such as died and dead are clearer than saying the baby is lost, asleep or has gone away. A young child may otherwise expect the baby to return or become frightened of sleeping. Explain simply that the baby’s body has stopped working and cannot start again: the baby cannot breathe, eat or feel pain now.

Describe the cause only as far as it is known and in words the child can understand. If doctors are still investigating, say that you do not yet know why it happened. Do not invent an explanation to fill the silence. Ask other caregivers to use the same basic account so that the child is not left trying to reconcile conflicting stories.

Expect questions to return

A child may ask when the baby is coming home after you have explained the death. They may ask the same question days or weeks later as their understanding develops. Answer patiently and check what they mean; a practical question about the baby’s body may need a short factual answer rather than a long discussion of every possible worry.

Understanding changes with development, experience and communication needs, not at one exact birthday. Use familiar language and, when helpful, pictures or other communication supports. Leave opportunities for questions during ordinary time together. If the child changes the subject or goes back to playing, you can stop and return later without treating that response as rejection.

Address guilt and fears about another death

Some children worry that jealous feelings, an argument or a wish not to share their parents caused the death. Ask gently what they think happened. Make clear that thoughts, wishes and feelings did not cause the baby to die. Reassurance should not require the child to confess a particular thought, behave perfectly or help adults feel better.

Children may also ask whether you or they will die. Listen to the fear rather than promising that nobody else can die. Explain what you truthfully know about the present situation and who is caring for them. Specific plans for school collection, bedtime and a familiar person to contact can offer reassurance without making an impossible guarantee.

Recognise different ways of grieving

Young children may become clingier, have disturbed sleep, wet the bed again or express feelings through play and behaviour. School-age children may alternate between questions, anger, sadness and ordinary activities. These are possible responses, not a checklist every child must follow. Laughter or a day with few visible tears does not tell you how much the baby mattered.

Teenagers may want privacy or prefer to talk with a trusted adult outside the immediate family. Offer that choice and keep contact open without demanding an emotional conversation. Notice changes in daily functioning and safety as well as words. You do not need to wait for a crisis to ask a child’s clinician or a bereavement service for advice.

Let them see feelings without carrying your grief

It is all right for a child to see you cry. Explain that you are sad because the baby died and that the child has not caused your tears. They do not have to cry too, comfort you or hide happiness to protect you. If a conversation becomes too much, another trusted adult can stay with them while you get support.

Seek adult help for your own grief and for practical tasks such as meals, travel and childcare. Older children should not become substitute parents or the family’s emotional caretaker. Keeping a little reliable time together can matter more than managing every task yourself. If distress is making ordinary care difficult, tell your healthcare or bereavement team.

Offer a choice about seeing the baby or saying goodbye

If seeing the baby is possible, discuss it with the care team before offering the child a choice. Ask staff how to explain what the child would see and what the baby may look or feel like. A child can choose not to look, touch or hold the baby. Contact is not necessary to prove love or to grieve properly.

Explain a funeral or other goodbye in concrete terms before asking whether the child wants to attend. Arrange a familiar adult who can accompany them and leave with them if needed. They can change their mind. Alternatives include choosing a drawing, flowers or a message, or taking part in a separate family moment; none is compulsory.

Keep everyday care predictable

Try to preserve familiar meals, school or nursery arrangements and bedtime habits where possible. Tell the child about changes and who will care for them. A favourite toy, ordinary play or quiet time with a trusted person may offer comfort. Predictability does not mean every day must look normal or that distress should be punished.

With appropriate attention to the child’s privacy and wishes, let school or nursery know what happened and what explanation has been used. Agree whom the child can approach and how staff will tell you about concerns. An older child may want help deciding what to say to classmates. Plans can be revisited as their needs change.

Make room for memories and ordinary happiness

Offer ways to remember without assigning tasks. A child might want to draw, write a letter, look at a photograph or keep a small memory box. Another may not want these activities now. Their choice can change. Avoid comparing them with an idealised version of the baby or suggesting that being cheerful means they have forgotten.

Birthdays, anniversaries, a new school year or a later family event may bring new questions. Ask what, if anything, the child would like to do on a significant date. Remembering can be quiet and personal; it does not require a cemetery visit or a ceremony. There is no deadline by which the family must stop mentioning the baby.

Ask for support when everyday life is becoming difficult

Contact the child’s healthcare professional or an experienced child bereavement service if their reactions concern you. Persistent or worsening problems with sleep or eating, strong withdrawal, difficulty attending school or a marked fall in usual functioning deserve assessment. These signs do not establish a diagnosis on their own, and support does not have to wait for a fixed number of weeks.

A professional can explore grief alongside other possible needs and discuss support for the child and family. Some children benefit from specialist counselling or mental-health care; not every bereaved child needs therapy. School and trusted adults can remain involved with suitable permission. Avoid making the child responsible for choosing or arranging all the help.

Take talk of wanting to die seriously

If a child says they want to die or join the baby, take the words seriously and seek urgent professional advice about their safety. Listen calmly rather than scolding them or assuming it is just grief. A healthcare professional or local urgent mental-health service can assess what they mean and what support is needed.

If the child has harmed themselves, taken an overdose, is in immediate danger or you cannot keep them safe, contact local emergency services or go to an emergency department now. Stay with them while arranging help. Do not wait for a routine bereavement appointment when safety is uncertain. The same immediate help is important if a parent or caregiver cannot stay safe.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Specialist bereavement organisations support honest, developmentally appropriate explanations and repeated opportunities for children to ask questions.

Goodbye and memory activities are personal choices. Recommendations here are supportive guidance, not a proven sequence that guarantees a particular grief outcome.

Child mental-health guidance distinguishes varied grief responses from concerning changes needing assessment; immediate safety concerns require emergency care.

How BeMama can help

BeMama can help you organise questions for your child’s healthcare, school or bereavement team. These adults can adapt support to your child’s understanding, communication needs and circumstances.

When to seek help

Seek urgent professional advice if a child talks about wanting to die. If anyone has harmed themselves, taken an overdose, is in immediate danger or cannot be kept safe, seek emergency help now and stay with them while arranging it.

Evidence notes updated: November 11, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Explain the death with short, truthful statements and make space for repeated questions.
  • Children may move between sadness, play, anger and ordinary enjoyment; there is no required grieving style.
  • Reassure them that thoughts and feelings did not cause the death, without promising nobody else can die.
  • Goodbyes, viewing and memory activities should be prepared choices, supported by trusted adults.
  • Maintain care and school connections; seek help for troubling changes and act immediately if anyone cannot stay safe.

Frequently asked questions

Should I tell a very young child that the baby died?

Use a short, clear explanation suited to their understanding, with help from a trusted adult if needed. Even children who cannot understand death fully can notice that something has changed. They may need the same explanation more than once.

What if I do not know why the baby died?

Say honestly that you do not know or that the doctors are still trying to understand. Give information when it becomes available in language your child can follow. Do not invent a cause or imply that the child’s thoughts or jealousy were responsible.

My child plays happily after talking about the baby. Is that wrong?

No. Children can move quickly between grief and ordinary play. They do not need to remain visibly sad to show love. Keep opportunities for conversation open and notice their overall wellbeing rather than judging one moment.

What if my child asks whether I will die too?

Acknowledge the worry and answer truthfully about what you know now. Do not promise that death can never happen. Explain who is caring for them and the practical plans for the day; repeated reassurance may be needed.

Must my child see the baby or attend the funeral?

No. Offer an informed choice where these options are available, prepare them for what to expect and provide a trusted adult who can leave with them. They may decline, change their mind or choose another way to say goodbye.

Is it harmful to cry in front of my child?

Tears can be explained simply: you are sad about the baby and the child has not caused your distress. They do not have to fix it or copy your reaction. Arrange adult support so they are not carrying responsibility for your wellbeing.

Should I tell the school or nursery?

Sharing relevant information can help staff support the child, use consistent explanations and notice difficulties. Consider the child’s privacy and wishes, especially as they get older, and agree a person they can approach when they need support.

When should I seek professional help?

Ask when you are worried, especially if difficulties with sleep, eating, relationships or school persist or worsen. Talk of wanting to die needs urgent advice. Immediate danger, self-harm, overdose or being unable to keep someone safe requires emergency help now.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
